segments.narration: Nobody ever found the manhole cover a nuclear test launched. Nevada, August 27th, 1957. A two-thousand-pound steel lid, welded over a borehole.
Underneath sat a bomb meant to barely fizzle. It yielded about three hundred tons instead. The shaft became a gun barrel.
A camera shooting a thousand frames a second caught the lid in exactly one frame. One. So how fast was it moving?
Los Alamos physicist Robert Brownlee ran the numbers and got six times Earth's escape velocity. He never recovered the cap.
It almost certainly never reached space. Compression heating would have vaporised the steel on the way up, which means the fastest thing humans had ever made burned itself out of existence.

verdicts.claim: No one ever recovered the steel cap launched up the shaft by the Pascal-B test at the Nevada Test Site on 27 August 1957.

verdicts.claim: Pascal-B yielded roughly 300 tons, far more than intended, and the blast travelled up the borehole.
verdicts.note: Listed at 300 tons and described as a failure of containment; secondary sources put the overshoot at about six times expectation.

verdicts.claim: A high-speed camera running about one frame per millisecond captured the steel cap in only a single frame.
verdicts.note: 69% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: Robert Brownlee of Los Alamos estimated the cap's velocity at about six times Earth's escape velocity, and it was never recovered.
verdicts.note: 86% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: Scientists believe compression heating vaporised the cap during its flight out through the atmosphere.
